0: Asking a model a question in a chat box is already familiar. What if you swap the keyboard for a microphone, ask out loud and wait for the answer to be spoken back?
1: This brings together several model types introduced earlier: ASR turns speech into text, the LLM answers, and TTS turns the text back into sound. When recording starts, whether the user has spoken and how the conversation history is saved all have to be arranged too.
3: A voice assistant needs to receive the user's spoken question, understand it, generate an answer and play that answer as speech. The ASR, LLM and TTS models do this work together.
5: ASR has to convert the audio signal captured by the microphone into text.
6: For example, the user says into the microphone “what famous sights are there in Beijing?”, and what the microphone captures is audio data:
8: The LLM cannot process this data as ordinary text, so ASR recognises the speech first and its result is passed on to the LLM as text input.
9: In a voice assistant, ASR has to care not only about whether the recognised content is right but also about accent, speed and background noise. The same sentence may be recognised differently in a quiet room and a noisy one.
11: The LLM takes the user's question text from ASR and generates the corresponding answer text. In a single-turn conversation the question goes in and the answer comes out fairly directly.
12: For example, ASR gives “what famous sights are there in Beijing?”, and after that text is sent to the LLM, the model produces: “Beijing's better-known sights include the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace and the Badaling Great Wall.”
13: Multi-turn conversation is different. For the LLM to resolve what the user's question refers to from the previous turn or turns, the earlier questions and assistant answers must be put into the context as well.
15: TTS converts the answer the LLM generated into speech, so the voice assistant can “say” the answer.
16: For example, for the LLM's answer “Beijing's better-known sights include the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace and the Badaling Great Wall.”, TTS turns it into audio:
18: The generated speech can be played straight through the speakers or saved as an audio file.
19: Besides reading the text correctly, TTS also affects how the assistant finally sounds. Whether the voice is clear, the pauses natural and the pace suitable all affect the real interaction experience.
20: In a voice assistant the TTS output is either non-streaming or streaming. If TTS waits for the LLM to finish the whole answer, the user clearly feels the wait. The better approach is streaming TTS: as the LLM generates a few characters, TTS immediately starts synthesising the corresponding audio segment and pushes it to the playback module, so it speaks while it generates.

88: Evaluating a voice assistant needs four mutually independent dimensions, each with one or more computable metrics: accuracy, latency, robustness and interaction naturalness.
90: Accuracy measures two things: whether the assistant “hears right” and whether it “answers right”.
91: The ASR word error rate (WER) is the hard metric for speech-to-text accuracy. It aligns the ASR output with a hand-annotated reference transcript by minimum edit distance, counts the substitutions (S), deletions (D) and insertions (I) and divides by the reference length N: WER = (S+D+I)/N. In real Chinese speech recognition, WER between 5% and 15% is an acceptable range; lower is better, but the optimisation cost rises exponentially.
92: The LLM answer semantic similarity measures how close the generated answer is to the reference answer in meaning. It uses BERTScore: a pre-trained language model encodes the generated answer and the reference answer into contextual vectors, the cosine similarity of each token vector in the two texts is computed and the overall score aggregated. BERTScore ranges from 0 to 1, and the closer to 1 the more consistent the meaning. Compared with traditional BLEU or ROUGE it tolerates synonymous phrasing better. For open questions that cannot be judged automatically, human scoring (out of 5) can be added.
94: Latency measures the processing speed of each stage and of the whole assistant, directly reflecting the system's computational efficiency.
95: The end-to-end total latency is the interval from VAD detecting the end of the user's speech (t_vad_end) to TTS finishing all audio output (t_tts_end), that is T = t_tts_end − t_vad_end. It reflects the user's whole wait from finishing speaking to getting the complete spoken answer.
96: The per-stage latency breaks the end-to-end total into four sub-stages:
97: VAD latency: from audio input to completing voice-activity detection
98: ASR latency: from extracting the speech segment to completing text recognition
99: LLM latency: from the user's text input to completing answer generation
100: TTS latency: from the answer text input to completing all audio synthesis
101: Record the start and end timestamps of each stage to locate bottlenecks. The sum of the four sub-stage latencies is the end-to-end total.
103: Robustness examines how much the assistant degrades under non-ideal conditions.
104: The evaluation builds several comparison test sets, each with the same question set but a different interference condition, and compares each result with the baseline (quiet room, standard Mandarin, normal speed), using the degradation as the quantitative basis for robustness.
105: Noisy environment: add three kinds of background noise (white noise, street noise, multi-speaker noise) to the original speech at three signal-to-noise levels (0 dB, 10 dB, 20 dB), record the WER and end-to-end latency at each level and observe how noise affects recognition accuracy and response speed.
106: Accent differences: collect or synthesise test speech with different dialect accents (such as Sichuan, north-eastern or Cantonese-inflected Mandarin) and compare with the standard-Mandarin test set; the WER difference directly reflects how far ASR is biased towards each accent.
107: Speaking-rate variation: use speech-processing tools to speed the test speech up to 1.3x and slow it to 0.7x and observe how WER fluctuates with the rate.
109: Interaction naturalness assesses whether the assistant behaves coherently and smoothly in multi-turn conversation.
110: The VAD error rate covers two mistakes: false triggers (VAD decides there is speech when the user is silent) and missed detection (VAD fails to detect the user speaking). False triggers make the assistant start recording and processing during silence, while missed detection cuts off the user's speech; both harm the experience. The evaluation runs continuously for 30 minutes in a real conversation and counts the proportion of frames where the VAD state disagrees with the hand-labelled true voice activity.
111: Multi-turn context retention: test whether the assistant can correctly resolve entities and intents mentioned earlier across 3-5 consecutive turns. For example, the user says in turn “how's the weather in Beijing today”, then “and Shanghai?”, then “which of the two is colder?”; the evaluation checks whether “and” in the second turn and “the two” in the third are resolved correctly. This metric cannot be computed automatically: a person must check each turn against the transcript, and the result is the proportion of correct turns.
112: The TTS naturalness MOS uses the Mean Opinion Score method to assess how natural the synthesised speech is. At least 10 listeners give subjective scores out of 5 to TTS samples (5 = indistinguishable from a real person, 1 = completely mechanical) and the arithmetic mean is taken. The samples must cover statements, questions, exclamations and both long and short sentences, at least 5 of each, to avoid bias from a single text type.
